intro: Hildegard’s Marian antiphon makes a complete setting from one melodic line. Follow the balance between syllabic declamation and the short groups of notes that extend a vowel.
question: How does Hildegard shape a prayer without adding a second voice?

sections.label: Marian antiphon · continuous solo line
sections.mNote: one complete prayer; no internal text boundary has been aligned

cues.title: One voice, several note-shapes
cues.text: Much of this antiphon gives each syllable one note, but short groups of notes sometimes prolong a vowel. Listen for those changes of pace within the single line, without an accompanying part to mark a beat.
cues.evidence: Beverly Lomer’s Hildegard Society commentary describes a primarily syllabic setting with neumatic elements and short melismas. Makemi’s source documents a solo live performance; no individual sung word is timed. https://www.hildegard-society.org/2014/10/o-frondens-virga-antiphon.html

cues.title: A particular manuscript witness
cues.text: O frondens virga survives in the Dendermonde manuscript, on folio 155r, but not in the expanded Riesencodex collection. It is a psalm antiphon for the Virgin, not a number from Hildegard’s drama Ordo virtutum.
cues.evidence: The Hildegard Society identifies the genre and manuscript witness and discusses the absence from the Riesencodex. This corrects the recording page’s erroneous dramatic attribution; the reason for the omission is not established.

cues.title: A melodic point of rest
cues.text: Across the prayer, notice how phrases return to a small number of anchoring notes. In the manuscript, D outlines most phrases and A provides a secondary centre: these are relationships within the melody, not chords sounded beneath it.
cues.evidence: Lomer identifies D mode and the phrase-defining D and A in the manuscript. These are written modal reference points, not an absolute-pitch claim about Makemi’s performance; the report’s E-minor estimate is not used to infer tuning or a transposition.
